subtitle: "A global symbol of resilience, forgiveness, and justice"

## Life After the Presidency

After leaving office in 1999, Mandela remained active in public life through
the **Nelson Mandela Foundation**, which he established to promote his
vision of social justice, and through humanitarian work focused on HIV/AIDS
awareness, rural development, and children's welfare via the Nelson Mandela
Children's Fund. He also played roles in international peace mediation,
including efforts related to the Burundian Civil War.

In 2009, the United Nations declared 18 July — Mandela's birthday —
**Nelson Mandela International Day**, inviting people worldwide to dedicate
67 minutes of their time to community service, symbolizing the 67 years
Mandela devoted to public service.

## Death and Global Mourning

Nelson Mandela died on 5 December 2013 at his home in Johannesburg at the
age of 95. His death prompted an outpouring of tributes from world leaders,
public figures, and ordinary citizens across the globe, and his state funeral
in Qunu, in the Eastern Cape, drew dignitaries from more than 90 countries.

## Enduring Influence

Mandela is widely regarded as one of the most significant political figures
of the 20th century. His life is frequently cited as a model of:

- **Moral leadership under extreme adversity** — maintaining his principles
  through 27 years of imprisonment without succumbing to bitterness.
- **Reconciliation over revenge** — choosing to build bridges with former
  adversaries rather than seek retribution.
- **Institution-building** — prioritizing durable democratic structures,
  including a constitutional court and an independent press, over
  personal power.
- **Global solidarity** — inspiring anti-colonial and civil rights movements
  well beyond South Africa's borders.

::: {.quote-block}
"No one is born hating another person because of the color of his skin, or
his background, or his religion. People must learn to hate, and if they can
learn to hate, they can be taught to love, for love comes more naturally to
the human heart than its opposite."
:::

Statues, streets, schools, and institutions around the world bear Mandela's
name, and his autobiography, *Long Walk to Freedom*, remains one of the most
widely read political memoirs ever published. Decades after his death, his
life continues to be studied as a case study in leadership, negotiation, and
the pursuit of a just and inclusive society.
